etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English sodeyn, sodain, from Anglo-Norman sodein, from Old French sodain, subdain (“immediate, sudden”), from Vulgar Latin *subitānus (“sudden”), from Latin subitāneus (“sudden”), from subitus (“sudden", literally, "that which has come stealthily”), originally the past participle of subīre (“to come or go stealthily”), from sub (“under”) + īre (“go”). Doublet of subitaneous. Displaced native Old English fǣrlīċ.

definitions.definition: Occurring quickly with little or no warning or expectation; instantly.

quote.citation: 1552, The Boke of Common Prayer [etc.]‎[1], The Letanie:
quote.text: From lightninges and tempeſtes, from plage, peſtilence, and famine, from battayle and murther, and from ſodayn death. / Good lord deliver us.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter I, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: I stumbled along through the young pines and huckleberry bushes. Pretty soon I struck into a sort of path that, I cal'lated, might lead to the road I was hunting for. It twisted and turned, and, the first thing I knew, made a sudden bend around a bunch of bayberry scrub and opened out into a big clear space like a lawn.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Hastily prepared or employed; quick; rapid.

quote.citation: c. 1599, William Shakespeare, Henry V, act 1, scene 1:
quote.text: Never was such a sudden scholar made.

Thus these pious flourishes and colours, examined thoroughly, are like the apples of Asphaltis, appearing goodly to the sudden eye; but look well upon them, or at least but touch them, and they turn into cinders.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XIV, page 22:
quote.text: And if along with these should come⁠The man I held as half-divine;⁠Should strike a sudden hand in mine,And ask a thousand things of home; […]I should not feel it to be strange.

quote.citation: c. 1591–1595, William Shakespeare, Romeo and Juliet, act 2, scene 2:
quote.text: I have no joy of this contract to-night: / It is too rash, too unadvised, too sudden;

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book VII”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Herbs of every leaf that sudden flowered.
